# PREFACE.

<image-desc>A rectangular woodcut headpiece with decorative floral and foliage motifs, featuring two central circular flowers surrounded by scrolling leaves.</image-desc>

There were no pagan philosophers <note>The author refers to "payens" (pagan) thinkers—those from the Greek and Roman traditions—to contrast their purely human reasoning with Christian revelation.</note> in ancient times who did not attempt to speak of the origin of the World. As they believed themselves obligated by their profession to give an account for everything, they would have been ashamed to admit that they were ignorant of the first principles of Nature. And furthermore, as they considered themselves strong enough, with their own reason alone <note>original: "lumieres" (lights), a common Enlightenment-era term for human intellect and rational capacity</note>, to penetrate its deepest mysteries and to dissipate all its obscurities, they boldly offered their opinions as certain truths.
   But just as there is perhaps no subject upon which they were so divided, there is also none in which they wandered further astray, or in which they more clearly jus-

He argues that their reliance on personal intellect led to conflicting theories and significant errors regarding the nature of the world.</summary>

<margin>13. That the first thing God made in the World was the primary matter of all bodies, and that this matter is finite.</margin>

He began with the production of matter, from which the whole [Universe] was to be made: God created first—that is to say, He made from nothing—a substance extended in length, width, and depth. In creating it, He placed it within that great space which the high heaven (of which we have just spoken) encloses within its concave surface; this is the same space occupied today by this marvelous machine <note>The author uses "machine" to describe the universe, a common 17th-century metaphor viewing nature as a complex, divinely-designed mechanism like a clock.</note>, which is entirely composed of that matter. 

Thus, He did not make it infinite—that is, absolutely without limits—since He enclosed it all within this boundary. Indeed, it was impossible for Him to make it infinite, for it is inconceivable that an extension <note>original: *étendue*. In the philosophy of this period (particularly Cartesianism), the defining characteristic of physical matter is "extension," or the fact that it occupies space in three dimensions.</note> could exist without some shape that limits it. He did not even make it indefinite—that is, without any limits that we can conceive—since it is easy for us to clearly conceive of this enclosure that contains it. But He made it of an astonishing size, for this enclosure where it is contained is immense, and there is no place within it that is not full.

# First Part.

<margin>14. *That even though this primary matter is everywhere the same, it can nevertheless be distinguished into three different species.*</margin>
It is indeed entirely of the same nature at its core: but nevertheless, because when God created it, He divided it all into an infinity of small parts, to which He gave at the same instant various movements, He made three different species from it. The first was a very subtle matter <note>original: *matiere tres subtile*. This refers to the finest grade of matter, which Descartes and his followers believed filled all voids and formed the stars and the sun.</note>, whose parts—born from the blunting of the small points or the small angles of that into which the primary matter had been first divided—were infinitely delicate, extremely agitated, without any determined shape, and very fit to exactly fill every kind of space. The second was that which was formed from those first parts of the primary matter that had been blunted and rounded; although these parts had some size and were very solid, they were nonetheless fine enough to be able to bear the name of subtle matter <note>This second element was thought to compose the heavens and allow for the transmission of light.</note>. Finally, the third species was a coarse matter <note>original: *matiere grossiere*.</note>, which was made from the first "very subtle" matter, several parts of which, having united together in various places, composed an infinity of small bodies of extremely different shapes and sizes.

*Whence it comes that among them there are some that are hot, cold, humid, and dry.*

For those whose parts were delicate, easy to stir, and to detach from one another by the action of the <term>subtle matter</term> <note>original: "matiere tres subtile." Part One. 93

...of fibers, which, originating from its stem <note>original: "queuë," referring to the pedicel or fruit-stalk.</note>, come together and intertwine beneath it, because the base prevents them from passing further. It is therefore necessary that the **sap** <term>suc: the nutrient-rich fluid or "juice" that circulates through a plant to provide nourishment</term> which arrives to make them grow—being unable to separate them to lengthen them—spreads them out and pushes them equally in all directions. Thus, it causes them to describe a **spherical shape**, just as we see that the air with which a bladder is filled rounds it out by pushing its membranes equally on all sides.

But the primary cause of this roundness in **fruits** comes from those juices which compose the **pulp**, and which make up its best and most significant part. For since this pulp which they compose always remains quite soft, and since many of its parts always remain liquid, it is not difficult for the **air**—which surrounds them and moves incessantly around them—to gather their particles into a round shape. It does this by pushing back toward the center all those particles that would tend to move away, just as it usually does to round the particles of **water** or any other liquid when, falling in small amounts, they are gathered immediately into **drops**.

<note>The author uses a mechanical argument common in the 17th century: that the internal pressure of fluids and the external pressure of air naturally dictate the geometric forms of nature.</note>

To do all these things, they had to be awake; that is to say, they had to have the fibers of their brain, and those of the nerves meant to lead to their sense organs, taut and capable of being shaken by the action of external objects. This is because it is in this disposition, of both the brain and the nerves, that wakefulness consists. For just as when a string is pulled tight, one cannot touch one end without moving the other; so, when the nerve fibers are properly taut, it is impossible for external objects to strike the end that leads to the sense organs without the action passing instantly to the other end. By shaking these nerve fibers, and the corresponding fibers of the brain, they create a sufficiently strong impression there. Indeed, it is within her bosom <note>original: "sein"; a poetic way of referring to the surface or interior of the earth</note> that most birds lay their eggs, sit upon them, and hatch them. Strictly speaking, it is also upon the Earth that all others make their nests—even those who build them on the roofs of houses and on the branches of trees—since the Earth supports these trees and houses upon which the nests are built. And if the <term>Halcyons</term> <note>Also known as Kingfishers; ancient naturalists believed these birds built floating nests on the sea during a period of calm weather called "Halcyon days"</note> make theirs upon the sea and raise their brood there, they are the only ones to do so and to multiply upon the sea; all others multiply upon the Earth.

<margin>All the operations of the Soul are nothing but modifications of its thought.</margin> [To] clearly recognize the truth of what we have said, that all its operations <note>In this context, "operations" refers to the active functions or processes of the mind.</note> are nothing but modifications of its general thought. For if all the Acts of its Understanding <term>Understanding: The intellectual faculty used for perceiving and processing information from the outside world.</term> are but perceptions that it has of external objects, which alter its state by impressing their ideas upon it, it is clear that all these Acts are but modifications of the natural feeling it has of itself. And if all those of its Will <term>Will: The faculty of the mind responsible for desire, choice, and initiating movement or change.</term> are but movements, which make it change its situation in regard to the objects that interest it, so that they no longer act upon it as they used to do, it is no less evident that all these Acts are likewise nothing more than modifications of this same general thought. Since, then, all its operations are reduced to these two kinds, and since all these operations are either Acts of the Understanding or Acts of the Will, it must necessarily be concluded that they are all only modifications of the natural feeling it has of itself and its state, and are various particular thoughts. But we must bring this truth into even greater light by explaining, in a few words, the nature of each of the principal operations of these two faculties of our Soul.

<margin>12. What the operations of the Understanding are, and how they are all equally thoughts.</margin>

Seven different kinds of operations are attributed to the Understanding: two that relate to the body, **sensing** and **imagining**; four that belong specifically to itself, **conceiving**, **judging**, **reasoning**, and **ordering**; and one that relates to both aspects, **remembering**. However, there is not one of these that does not consist of the perception of ideas which the Soul <note>The author uses "Soul" (French: *l’Ame*) here to mean the conscious mind or the thinking self.</note> feels are impressed upon it. For if the Soul perceives that it has within itself an idea that has come to it by way of a movement stirred in the brain of the body to which it is united—triggered by the action of external objects that have stimulated its organs—it **senses**. 

If it perceives that it has within itself an idea produced by a movement impressed on the brain solely by the movement of the animal spirits <term>animal spirits: A historical medical concept describing "subtle fluids" thought to travel through the nerves to facilitate sensation and muscle movement.</term> with which the brain is filled, it is said to **imagine**.

<term>Celestial Bodies</term> (Astres): General term for stars, planets, and the sun.
<term>Heavens</term> (Cieux): The celestial spheres.
<term>Astrologers</term> (Astrologues): Those who claim to predict the future via stars, here criticized.
<term>Earth</term> (Terre): The central focus of these celestial movements.
<term>Parallelism</term> (Parallélisme): The constant orientation of the Earth's axis.
<term>Solar Year</term> (An solaire): The time taken for one full circuit of the sun.
<term>Revolutions</term> (révolutions): The various movements or rotations of celestial bodies.

## ESTABLISHING THE TRUTH

### OF THE

## CHRISTIAN RELIGION.

<note>Vocabulary: Reflections, Genesis, Truth, Christian Religion</note>
<note>The term "Reflections" (original: "Reflexions") in the 17th and 18th centuries often denoted a series of scholarly or meditative essays intended to explore a subject deeply. Here, the author uses the first book of the Bible, Genesis, as the primary evidence to argue that the Christian religion is the intended fulfillment of ancient prophecies and divine history.</note>

<summary>This is the title page of a treatise that uses the Book of Genesis to provide a historical and spiritual defense for the validity of Christianity. It signals the author's intent to treat the biblical text as a foundational proof for religious doctrine.</summary>

<keywords>Title page, Genesis, Christian Apologetics, Biblical Truth, Theology</keywords>
